extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, MFA students, workshop participants
extracted.subtask_description: Craft guidance for writers of literary fiction and short stories, emphasizing how to earn insight, stage moral consequence, use stillness and patterning, and make objects and character contrasts carry weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earned insight (Against Epiphanies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of the workshop-fashionable Joycean epiphany: many stories present unearned moments of revelation that function as false closure. Quality fiction either truly earns an insight or deliberately refuses to provide one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'workshop epiphanies'—moments of revelation that are tacked on or insufficiently prepared. Build causal, emotional, or thematic work so that any revelation feels deserved; if you do not provide that groundwork, consider withholding the epiphany rather than offering a fraudulent one. Example anti-pattern: a sudden, tidy moral insight at the end that the preceding narrative hasn't justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral seriousness (without moralism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiction should stage real moral choice and consequence rather than skirt responsibility; moral seriousness is a quality, not preachiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray characters facing ethically meaningful decisions and show consequences rather than letting protagonists evade accountability. Do not slip into heavy-handed moralizing—let moral complexity emerge from character and situation. Anti-pattern: stories centered on protagonists who consistently avoid responsibility, yielding drift rather than moral stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stillness
rubrics_metrics.description: The deliberate use of moments where nothing apparently 'happens'—silence, pause, and atmosphere—as a craft element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stillness intentionally to create tension, interiority, or emotional weight rather than as inert filler. Allow pauses and quiet scenes to accumulate meaning; contrast stillness with action to make both more effective. Anti-pattern: relentless surface activity with no interior pauses, which flattens emotional resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patterning / Rhyming Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions and events in a story can echo, mirror, or refract earlier actions—creating underground harmonies akin to rhyme in poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design plot and character gestures so that later actions resonate with earlier ones (echoes, inversions, refrains) to produce a sense of cohesion and depth 'below conscious notice.' Avoid random or purely episodic events that lack structural or thematic echoes. Examples: deliberate repetition, mirrored decisions, symbolic correspondences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects with weight (Talking Forks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects in fiction (chairs, cups, photographs, utensils) can carry meaning beyond their practical function and serve as load-bearing presences in a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give objects associative, emotional, or symbolic heft by connecting them to character memory, desire, or theme. Make props do narrative work—anchor scenes, reveal interior life, or act as motifs. Anti-pattern: objects used solely for exposition or set-dressing with no deeper resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterpointed characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are often defined by contrast with one another; effective characterization frequently uses deliberate pairings and oppositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create character dynamics where differences illuminate desires, flaws, and values—use foils, mirror-characters, or contrapuntal relationships to reveal depth. Avoid isolated characters whose traits are asserted rather than shown through relational contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamiliarization
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying Shklovsky's principle: make the strange familiar and the familiar strange so readers see ordinary things anew.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fresh perceptions, unexpected angles, or language that disrupts habitual seeing to renew readers' engagement with everyday details. Balance novelty with comprehensibility so defamiliarization enriches rather than obscures meaning. Anti-pattern: novelty for its own sake that alienates readers without clarifying insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximalist aesthetics (the case for excess)
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument in favor of 'more'—density, expansiveness, and excess as legitimate aesthetic choices (exemplified by writers like Pynchon, DeLillo, Wallace).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate to project and voice, embrace abundance of material, digression, and complexity as expressive strategies. Ensure that scale and excess serve thematic or formal ends rather than becoming gratuitous; be mindful of readability and coherence. Not every story requires maximalism—use it when it deepens rather than distracts.
